name: Umar Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing electrical engineering with an industrial placement year later. A normal week is lectures, a lab where we wire and test small power circuits, and Friday prayers at the campus prayer room. I have my own room in a student flat ten minutes from campus. My dad pays, since he runs an electrical contracting firm with eleven staff.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the lab, and I like that I can wire a plug properly, which my flatmates can't. What wears me out is the theory, which is abstract. My school grades were average, mostly because I spent afternoons on site with my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's how it usually goes. I'd tell my flatmates that every few years something is going to change everything, and then work carries on. Online I'd say nothing, I'm not a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm pleased. My dad's firm would carry on, and so would I. Electricians are needed whatever happens, and my plan is to join him after the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd work at the firm in the holidays as I always do, and I'd apply to a big contractor for my placement year to see how larger jobs run. I'd also go to the mosque youth group on Sundays, which keeps my head straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the future I want, and it's not complicated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for explaining theory when the lecture lost me, and to check my calculations. I use it like a second textbook. I wouldn't use it for assessed work, because that's cheating, and I'd rather fail honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the family firm need in a plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady flow of jobs, good apprentices, and customers who pay on time. An electrician with a good name never runs out of work, because people ring the man who did it right last time.

I'd say nothing online, since I'm not a **poster**.
think: My dad's firm and I would both **carry on**; electricians are needed.
My plan is to **join him** after the degree.
do: Work at the **family firm** in the holidays as always.
Apply to a big **contractor** for my placement year to learn larger jobs.
feel: **Calm**: the future I want, and not complicated.

fieldNote: He uses AI as a **second textbook** but never for assessed work.

His long-term plan is simple and already set.

steps.text: Work holiday weeks at Dad's firm as usual
Apply to a big contractor for my placement year
Plan to join Dad's firm after graduating

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real but it's no reason to panic. I'd tell friends that skilled work with hands and good judgment will keep its value. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the quoting, scheduling, ordering and paperwork at my dad's firm would be done by software. That's about a third of what Dad's office manager, Mrs Okoye, does. The wiring in people's houses will still need someone to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help my dad try one scheduling tool and see if it saves time. I'd ask for a placement where I see design and site, so I'm useful in both. I'd also learn the basics of how to use AI to write quotes and check drawings, since I'd rather do that before competitors do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of unease for Mrs Okoye, who's worked there for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of your dad's work could software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything that's lots of paper. Quotes, invoices and stock orders. The physical work in someone's roof space isn't going anywhere soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your placement plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. Firms will need people who understand both the design side and the site, so I'd pick a placement that shows me both.

I'd tell friends skilled **hands and judgment** keep their value.
think: Quotes, scheduling and **paperwork** at Dad's firm will be done by software.
Wiring in houses still needs **someone** to do it.

Choose a placement showing both **design and site**, and learn AI for quotes.
feel: **Calm**, with some unease for Mrs Okoye, the office manager.

steps.text: Help Dad trial a scheduling tool at the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got to be ready for something big, and that families and mosques and churches have to look after each other. I'd say it plainly: don't wait for the government to arrive. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy. The thinking work of engineering would be done by AI by 2028, but wiring and fixing would carry on until about 2031. I'd have a degree that's partly worthless, but a trade that's very valuable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad about me joining the firm earlier, maybe after second year, and finish the degree part time. I'd learn electrical installation for real. I'd also help bring in tools to run the paperwork, so the firm is stronger when the change comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. I have somewhere to go, and many people won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what's the first thing you'd tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My trade gives me about three more years than a desk job, and I'd use every one of them to get skilled and save. That's what I'd tell him, and I'd ask for his advice on what to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your faith or community change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We'd organise as a community to help those who lose work, with food, advice and introductions to employers. A community that looks after its own doesn't have to wait for a handout.

say: I'd say we must be ready and that families and **mosques** should look after each other.
I'd tell people not to wait for the **government**.
think: The thinking part of engineering goes to AI by 2028, but **wiring** and fixing last to about 2031.
My degree would be **partly worthless**, but my trade very valuable.
do: Ask Dad to let me **join the firm** after second year and study part time.
Learn **installation** properly and bring in tools for the paperwork.
feel: **Uneasy**, not scared: I have somewhere to go.
S2.quote: A community that looks after its own doesn't have to wait for a handout.
fieldNote: Family firm is his **safety net**, and he knows many others lack one.
He prefers community help to handouts.
Plans to study part time to keep the qualification.

Help the mosque group set up a food and jobs service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fair heads-up. I'd tell friends to learn a skill they can use with their hands, plus a skill with their heads. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel steady. I'd graduate in 2029, work two years in the firm, and have a business running when the robots show up around 2034. It's tight, but I'd be ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the placement year, finish the degree, and join the firm with a plan. I'd buy a decent van and tools for myself as an investment. I'd save part of my pay and get my apprentices trained in the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some unease. I'd feel it's like being told a flood is coming in five years: you build higher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is the middle option. What do you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tools and a van, and training. If robots will do hands-on work in 2034, I'd rather own a firm that uses them than compete with one that does. I'd start learning how robots install things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd invest in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'd keep it practical. I'd rather buy equipment that earns than put money in shares I don't understand.

fieldNote: He treats robots as a **business** question: own the firm that uses them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's plenty of time to get ready. I'd tell friends to start something and not wait. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be quite relaxed. I'd be 28 with ten years of experience, probably running part of the firm, and the robots would come around 2039. I'd see them coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish, work, and take over more of the firm every year. I'd save, maybe buy a house, and marry, God willing. I'd stay in the mosque community and keep training younger workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is the kind of time you can build a life in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years feels comfortable. Is it too comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. People can slip when they think there's time. So I'd set goals for each year, so I don't drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the firm in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grow it a little each year, take on an apprentice or two, and bring in new tools when they're proven. I'd rather grow a firm slowly and keep my word than grow fast and cut corners.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture. The paperwork side would change fast, and I'd have barely started. What would help is skilled work that stays valued, apprenticeships, and communities that help each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm glad I have the firm. I know many classmates have no trade and no family business to fall back on, and I worry about them more than about myself.

headlineQuote: I know many classmates have no trade and no family business to fall back on, and I worry about them more than about myself.
portrait: **Umar** is 18, studies electrical engineering, and his dad, who runs an electrical contracting firm, pays for his flat.
He uses AI like a second textbook, never for assessed work, and spends holidays on site with his dad.
He stays calm in most worlds and uneasy when time is short, because the family firm is his safety net.
He values community, apprenticeships and free enterprise, and worries more about classmates than himself.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most: the firm's paperwork changes fast and he'd barely have started.
whatWouldHelp: Skilled work that stays valued, **apprenticeships**, and communities that help each other.
